A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Vec2Face research, with matching authors, architecture, and core experiments. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports original face-recognition experiments using generated HSFace datasets, scaling results, reconstruction comparisons, and main-text and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds IJBB/IJBC evaluations, larger-scale training results, identity-leakage experiments, and a stochasticity study.

M1.justification: The fMAE architecture, image decoder, discriminator, four-term training loss, PCA/Gaussian vector sampling, and AttrOP procedure remain unchanged. Revised projection and reshaping explanations and the new stochasticity discussion do not establish a new method component.

E1.justification: v4 retains the original nine verification test sets and adds IJBB and IJBC, described as more challenging and closer to real-world conditions. Their inclusion in the main comparison materially broadens evaluation coverage supporting the synthetic-versus-real claim.

E2.justification: Table 1 adds ID3 and removes Langevin-Disco while retaining most accuracy comparators. New appendix comparisons include DCFace and CemiFace for identity leakage (Table 12), plus reference models trained on the WebFace4M subset and Glint360K (Table 10).

E3.justification: New settings include IJBB/IJBC evaluation at TPR@FPR=1e-4, 400K-identity/20M-image training, larger real/synthetic mixtures, and five-million-identity leakage checks at thresholds 0.5 and 0.7. The existing 0.4-threshold overlap cleanup changes from removing identities to replacing them. v4 also reports an 80-epoch GAN-start setting after code optimization alongside the earlier 1,000-epoch setting, without identifying which retained results were rerun.

E4.justification: The earlier training-identity overlap check is expanded with cross-method and five-million-identity leakage analyses in Appendix A.8. v4 adds a repeated-generation study of fMAE stochasticity (Figure 14), extends scaling and mixed-training sensitivity tests, and revises interpolation and reconstruction case studies. Existing loss, attribute-control, and dataset-noise analyses remain.

E5.justification: New Figure 14 specifies eight generations per input vector to examine stochasticity. This adds limited repeated-inference reporting; neither version reports benchmark training seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests.

E6.justification: Existing HSFace10K and HSFace300K five-test averages remain 92.00% and 93.52%. New IJBB/IJBC results are 83.82%/86.96%, versus CASIA-WebFace's 78.71%/83.44% (Table 1). Table 2 adds HSFace400K at 93.24%, revealing a scaling decline. The reported training-overlap count changes from 168 to 1,194 identities, and Tables 10–13 add real-data reference, mixed-training, and leakage results.

T1.justification: The loss equations, perturbation equation, cosine-similarity constraints, and AttrOP mathematics are retained. Neither version provides formal theorems or proofs; the added leakage evaluations and mechanism discussion introduce no substantive mathematical development.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction extend the same-scale synthetic-over-real superiority claim from CALFW alone to CALFW, IJBB, and IJBC. The central claims of controllable synthesis, leading five-test accuracy, and successful scaling through 300K identities remain. Section 3.4 now explicitly characterizes the architecture as a minor contribution.

C2.justification: v4 adds substantive privacy and future-use discussion, acknowledges lower accuracy than the source real-data reference models, qualifies scaling benefits as continuing only through 300K identities, and discusses inference randomness. Appendix A.8 newly interprets similarity-threshold leakage results as establishing regulatory compliance or noncompliance; those broader conclusions are not established by the reported measurements.

D1.justification: v4 clarifies projected-feature handling, the decoder's 7x7x768 reshape, and inference stochasticity. It removes the project-code link and InsightFace configuration/access pointer supplied in v1. The detailed FR training configuration is retained, moving from Table 10 to Table 14.

R1.justification: Section 2 refines the contrast between static identity conditioning and perturbed input features. References add ID3, CemiFace, synthetic-FR challenges, VAE, privacy, and IJB sources, while removing Langevin-Disco and FaceStudio. The broader positioning against GAN and diffusion approaches remains.

P1.justification: There is extensive prose revision across the introduction, related work, novelty discussion, and experimental explanations. Method headings now distinguish architecture from inference procedures, terminology is corrected, and the appendix gains dedicated privacy, leakage, and supporting-material sections. These changes substantially revise exposition despite retaining the overall main-section sequence.

P2.justification: v4 redraws Figure 2, restructures and relocates main tables, adds IJBB/IJBC columns, and introduces Tables 10–13 and Figure 14. Appendix image grids are substantially recomposed and several plot panels reordered. The earlier fMAE diagram and training-configuration table are retained as Figure 15 and Table 14, rather than newly added.

improvement.justification: The harder IJBB/IJBC evaluations, disclosed 400K scaling decline, and added real-data and leakage comparisons improve evidence about efficacy and boundaries. The net gain is limited by removed code-access information and Appendix A.8's unsupported extension of similarity measurements into regulatory conclusions. Overall, empirical assessment becomes more informative, while important qualification and reproducibility issues remain.
